title: A Show-Me Week for the AI Trade
headline: Meta and Tesla report into a market that just sold good news; the Fed is silent; the 20-year auction and CCC spreads are the tells.
body:
### Setting the scene

Markets enter the week bruised but not broken. Last week the S&P 500 lost 2.0%, the Nasdaq-100 5.5% and semiconductors more than 10%. The 10-year Treasury is at 5.10%, WTI near $99 and the VIX at 20. The Fed's quiet period has begun ahead of its October 28 decision, so there will be no Fed speakers to talk markets up or down. That leaves earnings and data to steer.

### The big three questions

1. **Can Big Tech's numbers clear the bar?** Meta and Tesla report Wednesday. After a week in which ASML beat by 19% and still fell, we care less about the beat than about the capex outlook for next year. A Meta guide above consensus would tell us the AI build-out is still accelerating. A trim would feed the "digestion" story that hit chips last week.
2. **Does the bond market keep acting as a hedge?** Last week the 10-year fell 12bp while stocks dropped. Wednesday's 20-year auction, which last sold at 5.42%, tests whether real-money buyers are back at these yields.
3. **Is the CCC crack spreading?** CCC spreads widened 193bp in a month while BBs barely moved. If high yield as a whole widens another 25bp, we would treat that as a signal, not noise.

### Day by day

| Day | Data and events | Earnings |
|---|---|---|
| Mon Oct 19 | China Q3 GDP (4.4% y/y expected, 4.3% prior), industrial production and retail sales; Canada CPI (3.2% expected); NAHB housing index (31 expected) | |
| Tue Oct 20 | US housing starts (1.30m) and permits (1.40m); pending home sales; UK jobs; German ZEW | General Motors, RTX |
| Wed Oct 21 | UK CPI (3.4% expected); EIA oil inventories; 20-year Treasury auction | **Meta**, **Tesla**, AT&T, Elevance Health |
| Thu Oct 22 | Jobless claims (200k expected); Japan CPI (2.3% expected); 5-year TIPS auction; Kansas City Fed survey | Procter & Gamble, Union Pacific, Lockheed Martin, Valero, Comcast |
| Fri Oct 23 | Flash PMIs: US composite 57.6 expected (58.4 prior), plus UK and Germany; UK and Canada retail sales; CFTC positioning | American Express |

### What we're watching, by market

- **US equities:** speculators are net short S&P 500 futures (about −141,000 contracts) and trimmed Nasdaq longs last week. With positioning this light, good news from Meta could spark a sharp relief rally in tech. The more durable trade is breadth: equal weight and value have the momentum and the cheaper multiples.
- **Rates:** the 2-year at 4.74%, well above the 3.75%–4.00% funds rate, already prices further tightening. A soft housing week and a flash PMI near consensus would support the 10-year holding below 5.25%. TIPS remain our preferred way to own duration: breakevens of 2.35% look cheap with headline CPI at 3.7%.
- **Credit:** stay up in quality. BB and B bonds are positive for the year; CCCs are down 5.2%.
- **Commodities:** WTI rose 7.8% last week to $99. Wednesday's inventory report follows an 8.6-million-barrel draw. Energy remains the market's earnings tailwind and the consumer's headwind; staples' 5% rally last week says investors are paying up for defense.
- **International:** China's GDP print is the swing factor for EM after a 5.9% drop last week, much of it Korea's chip sell-off. The UK, a model preference, reports CPI, jobs and retail sales in one week.

### Looking further out

The following week is the heavyweight round:

- **October 28:** Microsoft and Alphabet report, and the FOMC announces its rate decision.
- **October 29:** Q3 GDP (3.1% expected) and September PCE inflation; the ECB also decides.
- **October 30:** the Bank of Japan decides.

### Bottom line

This is a show-me week for the AI trade and a test of whether bonds stay a hedge. Our base case is that strong earnings and 3%-plus growth keep the bull market intact while leadership keeps broadening. Our main risk flag is the weakest corner of credit. If Meta's capex guide holds up and high yield stops widening, we'd expect the S&P 500 to recover last week's losses before the Fed meets.

title: The Generals Retreated, the Troops Held
headline: The S&P 500 fell 2.0% as chips sank 10.5%, but the equal-weighted index rose and bonds rallied: a rotation inside a bull market, with a warning light in CCC credit.
body:
### The week in one paragraph

The S&P 500 fell 2.0% in its worst week since June, but the damage was concentrated. The Nasdaq-100 lost 5.5% and semiconductors 10.5%, while the equal-weighted S&P 500 *rose* 0.5% and Russell 1000 Value gained 0.9%. Consumer staples (+5.0%), energy (+4.9%) and health care (+3.5%) led. This was a rotation, not a rout: the generals retreated while the troops held their ground. Bonds did their job again, with the 10-year Treasury yield down 12bp to 5.10% as stocks slid. The VIX jumped 35% to 20.0, which is elevated but not panicked.

### Scoreboard

| Market | Level | Week | Year to date |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 (SPY) | 763.25 | −2.0% | +12.8% |
| Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) | 709.80 | −5.5% | +15.9% |
| S&P 500 equal weight (RSP) | 214.09 | +0.5% | +13.1% |
| Russell 1000 Value (IWD) | 255.77 | +0.9% | +22.9% |
| Russell 1000 Growth (IWF) | 121.48 | −5.0% | +2.9% |
| Russell 2000 (IWM) | 270.44 | −3.1% | +10.6% |
| Developed ex-US (EFA) | 103.55 | +0.2% | +9.5% |
| Emerging markets (EEM) | 62.85 | −5.9% | +15.5% |
| 10-year Treasury | 5.10% | −12bp | +92bp |
| High yield (HYG) | 76.86 | −0.5% | −0.3% |
| WTI crude | $99.02 | +7.8% | +72.5% |
| Gold | $4,181 | −0.8% | −3.7% |
| Dollar index | 101.66 | −0.4% | +3.7% |

### Chips down, staples up

The AI complex finally ran into the law of high expectations. ASML beat consensus EPS by 19% and TSMC by 3%, yet SMH dropped 10.5% and technology 7.7%. When beats get sold, the bar has moved above what even excellent results can clear. Korea, the market's purest memory-chip play, fell 15.1%.

We don't read this as the end of the AI cycle. Capex intentions on earnings calls are still rising, and AI and data centers came up on 81% of S&P 500 calls last season, against 69% a year earlier. What it does tell us is that leadership is broadening. The equal-weighted index beat the cap-weighted one by about 2.5 points in a single week. That's healthy for the bull market and painful for anyone overweight the top ten.

### Inflation: hot at the pump, cool underneath

- **Consumer prices:** September CPI rose 0.6% m/m and 3.7% y/y, as oil near $100 worked through. Core CPI rose 0.3% m/m and 2.6% y/y, which is not alarming.
- **Pipeline:** producer prices were the hot spot, up 1.3% m/m and 6.3% y/y, with core PPI up 0.7%. Import prices rose 1.1% m/m.
- **What bonds believe:** the 10-year breakeven is 2.35%, up only 7bp over the past year even as crude has roughly doubled. The market is treating the energy shock as a level shift, not a new inflation regime.
- **Who did the tightening:** the 10-year TIPS real yield rose 102bp over the year to 2.78%. Real rates are doing the Fed's work.

### Growth: no recession in these numbers

Headline retail sales rose just 0.1%, but sales ex-autos rose 0.9% and the year-on-year pace is 6.3% nominal. Industrial production jumped 0.7%, the Empire State survey surged to 25.5 (10.3 expected), and jobless claims held at 199,000. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow puts Q3 at 3.6%. The Philly Fed's slide to 20.9 from 37.8, with new orders down to 4.3, is the one soft spot worth watching.

### The Fed: Warsh keeps his options open

The Fed raised rates to 3.75%–4.00% in September, its first hike since 2023, and the median dot shows one more in December. This week Chair Warsh declined to pre-commit, and traders scaled back bets on an October hike. With core CPI at 2.6% and real yields near 2.8%, the case for a second hike is weaker than the September dots suggested. The FOMC announces its decision on October 28.

### Credit: watch the bottom of the stack

Investment grade spreads barely moved, at 84bp. High yield widened 8bp on the week and 47bp over the month to 323bp. CCC spreads blew out 193bp in a month to 1,278bp, within a few basis points of their widest in three years. The weakest borrowers are feeling 5% Treasury yields first. Year to date, CCCs are down 5.2% while BBs are up 0.3%. That divergence is our main risk flag.

### Earnings season: off to a strong start

Financials set a high bar:

- **Beats:** Goldman Sachs (EPS $17.01 vs $12.86 expected), BlackRock (+11%), Citigroup (+7%), Morgan Stanley (+3%), UnitedHealth (+13%), Johnson & Johnson (+3%).
- **Misses:** JPMorgan (−3%) and Bank of America (−2%), both modest.

The season's first 31 S&P 500 calls are running more upbeat than a year ago. Last season, 25% of companies mentioned raising guidance against 17% a year earlier.

### What the model says

The dashboard's allocation models still favor equities modestly: 67% against a 60% neutral, up from 66% a month ago. In fixed income they overweight TIPS and EM local-currency bonds against the Agg. In equities they prefer:

- **Regional banks:** 1.2× book value.
- **Oil & gas E&P:** at its 52-week high.
- **The UK:** 5.7% shareholder yield.
- **Global ex-US:** 11.3× forward earnings.

They avoid metals & mining, aerospace & defense and consumer discretionary. This week's rotation went the model's way.

### Bottom line

Our read is a rotation within a bull market, not the start of a bear market. Earnings are strong, the economy is running near 3.5% real growth, and long-run inflation expectations are anchored. The risks are 5% long yields, $100 oil and a CCC market that is cracking. We would use AI weakness to rebalance toward the broader market rather than to chase it lower, and keep a close eye on high yield.
